clinicalPearls: Constipation that develops or worsens on starting or increasing opioid therapy, with hard stools, straining and incomplete evacuation
Unlike many opioid effects, it does not reliably diminish with continued use (little tolerance develops)
It is a very common and often under-treated adverse effect that limits opioid therapy and quality of life
It is a component of the broader opioid-induced bowel dysfunction, which also includes reflux, bloating and cramping
Stimulant and osmotic laxatives are used first-line, with peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonists for refractory cases
It is distinct from narcotic bowel syndrome, in which the problem is worsening pain rather than constipation
reference.pathophysiology: Opioid-induced constipation results from opioid action on mu-opioid receptors in the enteric nervous system of the gut wall. This reduces propulsive peristalsis, increases non-propulsive tone and fluid absorption, and impairs the defecatory reflex, producing hard, infrequent stools and difficult evacuation. Because these peripheral gut receptors do not develop the tolerance seen with central analgesic effects, the constipation tends to persist throughout opioid therapy. Peripherally acting antagonists relieve it by blocking these gut receptors without reversing central analgesia.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical history linking constipation to opioid use
Assessment of stool pattern and abdominal and rectal examination
Exclusion of obstruction and metabolic causes where indicated
Review of the full medication list for other constipating drugs
Assessment of response to laxatives before escalating therapy
redFlags: Features suggesting bowel obstruction or faecal impaction with overflow
Failure to respond to appropriate laxative therapy
reference.prognosis: With appropriate laxatives and, where needed, peripherally acting antagonists, constipation is usually controllable, allowing continued analgesia; it persists as long as opioids are taken.
pitfalls: Failing to co-prescribe laxatives when starting opioids
Expecting tolerance to the constipating effect to develop
Confusing it with narcotic bowel syndrome
Missing faecal impaction with overflow diarrhoea
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Start stimulant and osmotic laxatives such as senna and macrogol first-line, given prophylactically at the outset of opioid therapy
Add a peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist such as naloxegol, methylnaltrexone or naldemedine for laxative-refractory cases, relieving constipation without reversing central analgesia
Consider opioid rotation or a combination oxycodone-naloxone preparation where symptoms persist
Advise non-pharmacological measures including adequate fluid intake, mobility and dietary fibre as tolerated
Review the medication list and reduce other constipating drugs
Exclude bowel obstruction and faecal impaction before escalating therapy
Reassess response and adjust the bowel regimen continuously, as tolerance to this effect does not develop while opioids are continued
